text: Welcome to Retry Side Effects. The big idea for today is that a design can look perfectly fine when it runs once, but still fail when retries, timing pressure, or partial failure are introduced. We are going to focus on how to recognize the hidden assumption, how to produce evidence of the failure, and how to defend a correction without pretending the fix is free.

The key idea here is that a system can appear correct in the happy path and still be fragile under retry pressure. A single clean run does not prove the design is safe. What matters is whether the same workflow still behaves correctly when workers fail, messages are redelivered, or state changes happen in the middle of processing. That is why evidence has to survive failure, not just success.

Retry storms happen when many failed workers all try again at about the same time. Instead of recovering, the system can suddenly create a spike in downstream load. That can produce duplicate work, make progress slower, and even stall the whole pipeline. A common mistake is treating retry as a harmless implementation detail. In reality, retries become a design pressure on queues, workers, and shared resources.

Imagine a set of workers all failing together and then retrying together. The downstream service gets hit repeatedly instead of recovering gradually. The retry queue becomes part of the failure path, not just a convenience. The professional question is whether the system can absorb that pressure without duplicating work or blocking progress. If the answer depends on luck, the design is not ready.

Partial success is especially uncomfortable because the worker has already done some real work before the failure. Maybe it wrote a file, charged a card, or published part of a message, and then crashed before finishing. On retry, the same action may be attempted again, which can create duplicates or conflicts. This matters because the failure is hidden in the gap between 'started' and 'completed,' and that gap is exactly where retries become dangerous.

Here the important point is that retrying a half-finished operation can repeat the side effect instead of completing it safely. If the first attempt wrote fifty percent of a file and then died, the next attempt may not know what was already done. That is how you get a duplicate write, a clash, or a corrupted workflow. The lesson is to make partial completion visible in the design, not just assumed away.

Zombie resources are the leftovers that keep existing because retries created more than one copy of something. Think about cloud VMs, temporary files, or jobs that were started twice and never fully cleaned up. The cost often grows quietly, which makes this problem easy to ignore at first. But from an engineering perspective, cleanup is part of the design, not an afterthought.

The point here is that repeated retries can create orphaned resources that linger longer than expected. A retry loop may create one VM, then another, and maybe a temporary file too, while cleanup arrives late or not at all. That leads to wasted cost and confusing operational state. A mature design has to account for those leftovers explicitly, because the system is not just doing work once; it is managing the consequences of repeated attempts.

Let's pause here and name the discipline that protects you from bad retry assumptions: state the invariant first. Before you pick a lock, a queue, a key store, or a backoff policy, you need to say what must remain true. Tool names are not invariants. The invariant is the meaning you are trying to preserve, and the mechanism is chosen second to protect that meaning.

The key idea is that the invariant connects the claim, the logs, and the test. If you know what must stay true, then you can choose a control that protects it, capture evidence that records it, and repeat the test to prove it. If you skip that step, you end up defending a mechanism instead of defending correctness. That is a common mistake in design reviews.

Think about a normal workflow where checkout publishes a shipping event, a queue delivers it, a worker checks an idempotency store, and then the worker performs the notification before acknowledging the message. The important property is not just that messages move through the pipeline, but that the worker knows whether this event has already been handled. That is how you design for delivery uncertainty instead of pretending delivery is exactly once.

This state model makes the workflow explicit. An event starts enqueued, gets delivered, moves into processing, then completes, and finally gets acknowledged. But there is also a retry pending path if the worker crashes before finishing. The invariant is that each external side effect for an order event is applied at most once, even if delivery happens more than once. That is the property we care about protecting.

Now imagine the uncomfortable interleaving: Worker A ships order forty-two and crashes before the acknowledgement is recorded. The queue redelivers the same event to Worker B, and Worker B ships it again. That creates duplicate shipment, and the log may never show a clean completion path. This is hidden in the baseline because the happy path assumes delivery count and execution count are the same thing, but under pressure they are not.

The failure signal is concrete: duplicate shipment, missing acknowledgement, stale state, and broken progress. A reviewer should be able to reconstruct that from logs, trace IDs, and the invariant being defended. If the evidence is vague, then the claim is weak. The goal is to make the failure observable enough that another engineer can tell exactly what happened and why it violates the expected property.

When you are reviewing a retry failure, ask whether the evidence actually supports the claim. If the logs say duplicate event nine and the trace IDs connect that event to order forty-two, then you can reason about the invariant. If the reviewer cannot connect the side effect to the event and the state transition, the evidence is not strong enough. This is why structured logs and correlation matter so much.

A safer design uses idempotency keys, durable completion records, retry-safe handlers, and reconciliation scans. The protected property is simple to state: retried events should not inflate side effects or hide lost work. The trade-off is that safety is not free. You pay with extra storage, more state to manage, and more careful handler logic, but that cost is what buys you correctness under retry pressure.

Here the mechanism is doing real work. The worker claims a key once, the key store rejects repeated claims, the side effect is performed, and completion is recorded durably before the retry can re-enter. That makes a retry safe rather than harmful. But it also means the handler is more complex, and you need to think about what happens if the worker succeeds but the acknowledgement is lost. The fix protects the invariant, but it does not eliminate operational trade-offs.

This comparison is meant to guide judgment. A baseline design is easy to explain, but it often hides timing assumptions. A guarded design protects the invariant directly, but it requires careful modeling. An idempotent design survives retries, though it needs keys or deduplication. An observability-first design gives you stronger evidence, but it adds logging work. The right choice depends on what failure you need to defend against.

The evidence flow matters because a claim about retry behavior has to be reconstructable. Operation IDs, entity IDs, repeatable runs, and traces all help the reviewer verify what happened. A good test does not just pass once; it can be repeated under pressure and still produce the same failure or the same recovery behavior. That is what makes the conclusion defensible.

This is the bridge to A3. You need to show the invariant, show the failure, show the fix, show the evidence, and defend the trade-off. In your project, that means identifying the relevant object, workflow, event, or recovery mechanism in your own domain, then proving with evidence that the design behaves correctly under pressure. Your Integrity Packet should make the assumption, validation, and remaining risk explicit.

The final connection to A3 is that your submission should not just describe a solution, but defend it with a full evidence chain. Show the baseline behavior, show the pressure condition, show the corrected behavior, and explain why the chosen control preserves the invariant. Then tie that reasoning back to your Integrity Packet so the reviewer can see the assumption, the validation, and the remaining risk all in one place.

Let's end with two questions worth discussing. First, what breaks first under retries in your own system: correctness, progress, or cost? Second, which trade-off would you actually accept if you had to defend the design in review? Those answers usually reveal whether the system is built for the happy path only, or whether it is ready for real operational pressure.
